newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin faces busy agenda, emotional burden.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin faces busy agenda, emotional burden.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin will have an extremely busy agenda in the coming weeks, according to a schedule announced on Tuesday by his press secretary, Sergei Yastrzhembsky.
On Thursday, the 66-year-old Kremlin leader will chair a meeting of his Defence Council which could mark the start of much delayed military reform.
Also on Thursday, Yeltsin will meet Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko to remove differences over a charter, to be signed on Friday, to a union treaty agreed last month.
On the same day, Yeltsin will chair the first meeting of the four top officials in the country -- himself, the prime minister and the speakers of both chambers of parliament.
Such meetings have been proposed by the president to promote cooperation between the legislative and executive powers.
And he will also meet Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda on Friday to discuss bilateral relations and the June summit of the Group of Seven (G7) rich industrial nations and Russia.

Next Monday, Yeltsin leaves for Paris to sign a treaty with NATO which outlines relations between the two once the Western defence alliance invites some of Moscow's former Warsaw Pact allies in eastern Europe to join it.
While in France, Yeltsin will have bilateral meetings with the leaders of the United States, France and Britain.
And on May 30 Yeltsin will head for Ukraine on a visit which is likely to be marked by the long-delayed signing of a sweeping accord between the two Slav neighbours.
The visit has been postponed many times due to a dispute over the former Soviet Black Sea fleet.

The busy agenda highlights Yeltsin's firm grip on power after he recovered from heart surgery last November and double pneumonia in January. The U.S. surgeon who advised on the operation said on Tuesday he was recovering ahead of schedule.

Yeltsin will also have to keep a close eye on reforms pursued by his new government whose short-term programme he approved on Monday. The reforms may be painful for many and unpopular. Realising that, the president pledged to throw his weight behind the programme and back it fully.
The beginning of this week must have presented a heavy emotional burden on Yeltsin, evoking memories of August 1991.
Then the newly elected Russian leader led resistance from the White House parliament building to a hardline coup attempt which briefly ousted Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev.
The man who headed the military defence of the White House with several dozen men against a possible tank or airborne attack was Konstantin Kobets.
The stocky general enjoyed Yeltsin's confidence and made headlines after the coup leaders were arrested.
"I will be happy only when I lead the firing squad which will execute those scoundrels," Kobets told reporters.
Kobets was a hero then and the decision to sack him as deputy defence minister and chief military inspector, announced on Tuesday, must have been a difficult one for Yeltsin.
Kobets is charged with bribe-taking and abuse of power.

But Yeltsin may have some happier memories later on Tuesday when he goes to a concert honouring another hero of 1991 -- cellist Mstislav Rostropovich. The concert is part of celebrations of the musician's 70th birthday.
The world-renowned maestro, forced into exile by the Soviet authorities, flew to Moscow in August 1991 to support Yeltsin and the resistance to the coup.
